title: India Urges Middle East De-escalation, Condemns Attacks on Ships and Civilians
excerpt: At the UN Security Council, India stood with Saudi Arabia, condemned strikes on airports and seafarers, and called for restraint after an Indian engineer was killed in Riyadh.
body:
• India told the UN Security Council it stands in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and called for restraint and de-escalation in the Middle East.
  • India condemned repeated attacks on civilian infrastructure, including Saudi airports, and on maritime navigation and seafarers.
  • An Indian citizen, Mohammad Yousef Ali, an IT engineer from Hyderabad, was killed in the attack on Riyadh airport.
  • For Indian seafarers and Gulf-based workers, India stressed protection of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and Southern Red Sea as a shared international responsibility.

India has urged restraint and de-escalation in the Middle East and condemned attacks on civilian infrastructure, ships and seafarers, in remarks at the United Nations Security Council's quarterly open debate on the region. India's Permanent Representative P. Harish said the escalation in hostilities was deeply worrying and had become a principal challenge facing the international community, according to IANS.

Harish said India stands in complete solidarity with the government and people of Saudi Arabia in defence of their sovereignty, after a series of attacks attributed to the Houthis, the Iran-aligned Yemeni group fighting Yemen's internationally recognised government. He did not name the group in the remarks reported by IANS.

An Indian Life Lost in Riyadh

The attacks have a direct Indian cost. Harish told the Council the strikes on civilian infrastructure, including Saudi airports in recent days, had led to the loss of lives, including that of an Indian citizen, Mohammad Yousef Ali, in Riyadh. Ali, an IT engineer from Hyderabad, was killed on Saturday while on a pilgrimage, in the attack on Riyadh airport, IANS reported.

India reaffirmed its commitment to the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and rejected interference in its internal affairs, positioning its statement as support for both Saudi sovereignty and a Yemeni settlement rather than for escalation by any side.

"We strongly condemn attacks on maritime navigation and on the seafarers, many of whom are Indian citizens."

— P. Harish, India's Permanent Representative to the UN

Shipping Lanes and Seafarers

Maritime security was the second strand of India's case. With the Strait of Hormuz already under strain from attacks on shipping and the resulting pressure on energy supplies, Harish said the Houthis had opened a new front in the Red Sea. Protection of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Southern Red Sea, he said, is a shared international responsibility and a global interest.

That is not abstract for India. Indians form one of the largest national groups in the global seafaring workforce, and millions of Indian citizens live and work across the Gulf. Attacks on merchant vessels and on airports used by migrant workers and pilgrims put both groups at direct risk, and disrupt the energy shipments on which India's economy depends.

Dialogue Over Escalation

India's broader position, also reflected in its statement at the Council reported by the Times of India, is that the conflict should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy. Harish called for restraint from all sides and de-escalation, rather than retaliation that widens the theatre from Yemen and Saudi Arabia into the Red Sea shipping corridor.

For Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere in the Gulf, the practical advice remains to follow Indian embassy advisories, monitor flight schedules that have been disrupted by airport attacks, and for seafarers, follow company and flag-state routing guidance through the Bab al-Mandab and Hormuz corridors.

What to Watch

Whether the Council debate produces any collective call for a ceasefire, and whether attacks on Saudi airports and Red Sea shipping pause, will determine if India's appeal gains traction. For now, New Delhi has placed three markers publicly: solidarity with Saudi Arabia, condemnation of attacks on civilians, ships and seafarers, and a demand that the sea lanes Indians depend on be protected.
